{{Short description|Concept in explosives engineering}}
[[File:Chapman Jouguet.svg|thumbnail]]
The '''Chapman–Jouguet condition''' holds approximately in [[detonation]] waves in [[high explosive]]s. It states that the detonation propagates at a [[velocity]] at which the reacting gases just reach [[sonic velocity]] (in the frame of the leading [[shock wave]]) as the reaction ceases.<ref>{{citation |last=Cooper |first=Paul W. |title=Explosives Engineering |location=New York |publisher=Wiley-VCH |year=1996 |isbn=0-471-18636-8}}</ref><ref>{{citation |first1=Wildon |last1=Fickett |first2=William C. |last2=Davis |title=Detonation |publisher=U. Calif. Press |location=Berkeley |year=1979 |isbn=0-520-03587-9}}</ref>

[[David Chapman (scientist)|David Chapman]]<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Chapman | first1 = D. L. | title = VI.On the rate of explosion in gases | doi = 10.1080/14786449908621243 | journal = [[Philosophical Magazine]] |series=Series 5 | volume = 47 | issue = 284 | pages = 90–104 | year = 1899 | url = https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=pst.000068486822;view=1up;seq=104 | url-access = subscription }}. Also [https://archive.org/details/londonedinburgh5471899lon Archive.org]</ref> and [[Émile Jouguet]]<ref>{{citation |last=Jouguet |first=Emile |title=Sur la propagation des réactions chimiques dans les gaz |trans-title=On the propagation of chemical reactions in gases |language=fr |journal=[[Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées]] |series=series 6 |volume=1 |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k107470r/f353.image |pages=347–425 |date=1905}}<br />{{citation |last=Jouguet |first=Emile |title=Sur la propagation des réactions chimiques dans les gaz |trans-title=On the propagation of chemical reactions in gases |language=fr |journal=Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées |series=series 6 |volume=2 |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k1074714/f8.image |pages=5–86 |date=1906}}</ref> originally (c. 1900) stated the condition for an [[infinitesimally]] thin detonation. A physical interpretation of the condition is usually based on the later modelling (c. 1943) by [[Yakov Borisovich Zel'dovich]],<ref>{{cite journal |last= Zel'dovich |first= Yakov Borissovich |author-link=Yakov Borisovich Zel'dovich |date= 1940 |title= К теории распространения детонации в газообразных системах |trans-title= On the theory of the propagation of detonation in gaseous systems |journal=[[Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Physics]] |volume= 10 |pages= 542–568 }}  Translated into English in: ''National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics Technical Memorandum'' No. 1261 (1950).</ref> [[John von Neumann]],<ref>See:
* {{citation |last=Neumann |first=John von |author-link=John von Neumann |title=Theory of detonation waves |publisher=Office of Scientific Research and Development |id=Report No. 549, Ballistic Research Laboratory File No. X-122 |location=Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland |date=1942 |url=https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/citations/ADB967734}}
* Progress Report to the National Defense Research Committee, Division B, OSRD-549 (April 1, 1942.  PB 31090) 34 pages. (4 May 1942).
* {{Citation |first=John |last=von Neumann |author-link=John von Neumann |title=John von Neumann, Collected Works |editor-first=A. J. |editor-last=Taub |volume=6 |chapter=Theory of detonation waves |location=Elmsford, N.Y. |publisher=Permagon Press |year=1963 |orig-year=1942 |isbn= <!-- 0080095666 isbn for vol 1 --> |pages=178–218}}</ref> and [[Werner Döring]]<ref>{{cite journal|last= Döring |first=Werner |date=1943 |title=Über Detonationsvorgang in Gasen |trans-title= On the detonation process in gases |journal= Annalen der Physik | volume=43 |issue=6–7 |pages=421–436 |doi=10.1002/andp.19434350605|bibcode = 1943AnP...435..421D }}</ref> (the so-called [[ZND detonation model]]).

In more detail (in the ZND model) in the frame of the leading shock of the detonation wave, gases enter at supersonic velocity and are compressed through the shock to a high-density, subsonic flow. This sudden change in pressure initiates the chemical (or sometimes, as in [[steam explosion]]s, physical) energy release. The energy release re-accelerates the flow back to the local speed of sound. It can be shown fairly simply, from the one-dimensional gas equations for steady flow, that the reaction must cease at the sonic ("CJ") plane, or there would be discontinuously large pressure [[gradient]]s at that point.

The sonic plane forms a so-called choke point that enables the lead shock, and reaction zone, to travel at a constant velocity, undisturbed by the expansion of gases in the [[rarefaction]] region beyond the CJ plane.

This simple one-dimensional model is quite successful in explaining detonations. However, observations of the structure of real chemical detonations show a complex three-dimensional structure, with parts of the wave traveling faster than average, and others slower.  Indeed, such waves are quenched as their structure is destroyed.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Edwards, D.H. |author2=Thomas, G.O. |author3=Nettleton, M.A. |name-list-style=amp |title=The Diffraction of a Planar Detonation Wave at an Abrupt Area Change|journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics|volume= 95|issue=1|pages =79–96|year= 1979|doi=10.1017/S002211207900135X|bibcode = 1979JFM....95...79E }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.2514/5.9781600865497.0341.0357 |volume=75 |journal=Progress in Astronautics & Aeronautics|year=1981|title=Diffraction of a Planar Detonation in Various Fuel-Oxygen Mixtures at an Area Change|isbn=978-0-915928-46-0|pages=341–357|editor=A. K. Oppenheim |editor2=N. Manson |editor3=R.I. Soloukhin |editor4=J.R. Bowen|author1=D. H. Edwards |author2=G. O. Thomas |author3=M. A. Nettleton }}</ref>  The Wood–Kirkwood detonation theory can correct for some of these limitations.<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1007/s00214-007-0303-9 | title = Improved wood–kirkwood detonation chemical kinetics | year = 2007 | last1 = Glaesemann | first1 = Kurt R. | last2 = Fried | first2 = Laurence E. | journal = Theoretical Chemistry Accounts | volume = 120 | pages = 37–43|issue=1–3| s2cid = 95326309 | url = https://zenodo.org/record/1232641 }}</ref>

==Mathematical description==
Source:<ref>Williams, F. A. (2018). Combustion theory. CRC Press.</ref>

The '''Rayleigh line''' equation and the '''Hugoniot curve''' equation obtained from the [[Rankine–Hugoniot conditions#Simplified Rankine-Hugoniot relations|Rankine–Hugoniot relations]] for an [[ideal gas]], with the assumption of constant specific heat and constant molecular weight, respectively are
:<math>\begin{align}
  \frac{\tilde{p} - 1}{\tilde{v} - 1} &= -\mu \\
                            \tilde{p} &= \frac{[2\alpha + (\gamma + 1)/(\gamma - 1)] - \tilde{v}}{[(\gamma + 1)/(\gamma - 1)]\tilde{v} - 1},
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>\gamma</math> is the [[specific heat ratio]] and

:<math>
  \tilde p = \frac{p_2}{p_1},\quad
  \tilde v = \frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}, \quad
    \alpha = \frac{q\rho_1}{p_1}, \quad
       \mu = \frac{m^2}{p_1\rho_1}.
</math>

Here the subscript 1 and 2 identifies flow properties (pressure <math>p</math>, density <math>\rho</math>) upstream and downstream of the wave and <math>m</math> is the constant [[mass flux]] and <math>q</math> is the heat released in the wave. The slopes of Rayleigh line and Hugoniot curve are

:<math>\begin{align}
  \frac{d\tilde p}{d\tilde v} &= \frac{\tilde{p} - 1}{\tilde{v} - 1}, \\[3pt]
  \frac{d\tilde p}{d\tilde v} &= -\frac{[(\gamma + 1)/(\gamma - 1)]\tilde{p} + 1}{[(\gamma + 1)/(\gamma - 1)]\tilde{v} - 1}.
\end{align}</math>⋅

At the Chapman-Jouguet point, both slopes are equal, leading the condition that

:<math>\tilde p = \frac{\tilde v}{(\gamma + 1)\tilde v-\gamma}.</math>

Substituting this back into the Rayleigh equation, we find

:<math>\mu = \gamma\frac{\tilde p}{\tilde v}.</math>

Using the definition of mass flux <math>m \equiv \rho_1 u_1 = \rho_2 u_2</math>, where <math>u</math> denotes the [[flow velocity]], we find

:<math>M_2 = \frac{u_2}{c_2} = 1</math>

where <math>M</math> is the [[Mach number]] and <math>c</math> is the [[speed of sound]], in other words, downstream flow is sonic with respect to the Chapman-Jouguet wave. Explicit expression for the variables can be derived,

:<math>\begin{align}
  \tilde{p}_\pm &= 1 + \alpha(\gamma - 1)\left\{1\pm\left[1 + \frac{2\gamma}{\alpha\left(\gamma^2 - 1\right)}\right]^\frac{1}{2}\right\},  \\
   \tilde v_\pm &= 1 + \frac{\alpha\left(\gamma - 1\right)}{\gamma}\left\{1 \mp \left[1 + \frac{2\gamma}{\alpha\left(\gamma^2 - 1\right)}\right]^\frac{1}{2}\right\}, \\
        \mu_\pm &= \gamma + \alpha(\gamma^2 - 1)\left\{1 \pm \left[1 + \frac{2\gamma}{\alpha\left(\gamma^2 - 1\right)}\right]^\frac{1}{2}\right\}.
\end{align}</math>

The upper sign applies for the '''Upper Chapman-Jouguet''' point ([[detonation]]) and the lower sign applies for the '''Lower Chapman-Jouguet''' point ([[deflagration]]). Similarly, the upstream Mach number can be found from

:<math>M_{1\pm} = \left[1 + \frac{\alpha\left(\gamma^2 - 1\right)}{2\gamma}\right]^\frac{1}{2} \pm \left[\frac{\alpha\left(\gamma^2 - 1\right)}{2\gamma}\right]^\frac{1}{2}</math>

and the temperature ratio <math>\tilde{T} = T_2/T_1</math> can be found from the relation <math>\tilde{T} = \tilde{p}\tilde{v}</math>.
